articles.title: Trump's latest claim about his economy immediately backfires: 'Not how this works'
articles.description: President Donald Trump's latest claim about his economy immediately backfired Tuesday. Speaking with reporters outside the White House , Trump said that his economic policies had produced a "strong dollar." Usually, that term means U.S. imports are cheaper, and exports to foreign countries are more expensive. But Trump was using the phrase to refer to a different problem altogether, one that several of his critics noted was completely irrelevant. "We have a very strong dollar. That's because we're doing well. A strong dollar is good in many ways. I guess you could make the case that a strong dollar slows things down, but a strong dollar gives you a lot of life," Trump rambled. "And, you know what a strong dollar does? It gives you no inflation." Trump's comments seem to belie the reality presented in his administration's economic data. In August, inflation jumped 3.4%, driven by the rising cost of gasoline, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For comparison, the inflation rate was measured at 3%. Trump's critics reacted to his comments on social media. "Um... That's not how this works. That's not how any of this works," Pradheep Shankar, a National Review contributor, posted on X. "Wharton should be investigated for fraud for giving this idiot a degree," Spencer Hakimian, founder of Tolou Capital Management, posted on X. "Alright. Thanks," Ed Zitron, CEO of EZPR.com, posted on X. Trump: We have a strong dollar because we are doing well. You know what it does? It gives you no inflation. https://t.co/9DmhYpVU3l — Acyn (@Acyn) October 6, 2026

articles.title: US oil inventory preview: five terms to know before Wednesday's EIA data
articles.description: US oil inventory preview: five terms that explain what traders will be watching US crude stockpiles are expected to have risen last week while fuel inventories fell, a Reuters poll showed. Early industry data, however, points the other way on crude. Here's what's expected, and what the key terms in the weekly reports actually mean. What analysts expect Analysts polled by Reuters expect crude inventories to have risen by close to 2 million barrels in the week to 2 October, roughly in line with the five-year average for the time of year. Gasoline stocks are seen falling by a similar amount and distillate stocks by about 2 million barrels. Refinery utilisation is expected to have slipped slightly from about 92.5% of capacity. The previous week's official data surprised the market. Crude stocks rose by about 900,000 barrels to around 427 million, when analysts had expected a small draw. What the API showed The American Petroleum Institute's figures, released after Tuesday's settlement, pointed in a different direction. According to market sources, the API reported a crude draw of about 2 million barrels , against expectations for a build. Gasoline stocks fell by about 1.4 million barrels, while distillates rose by roughly 460,000 barrels. The API data comes from a voluntary industry survey and often differs from the government's figures. The official Energy Information Administration report is due on Wednesday at 10:30 am ET (14:30 GMT) and is the market's benchmark. The terms explained Crude inventories. This is the volume of unrefined oil held in commercial storage across the US, at tank farms, terminals and refineries. It excludes the government's Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is reported separately. A rise is called a "build" and suggests supply is outpacing what refiners need. A fall is a "draw" and suggests the market is tightening. Gasoline stocks. Gasoline is the largest single product made from US crude, so stock levels are a direct read on consumer fuel demand. Falling gasoline stocks with refineries running steadily usually point to solid demand at the pump. Distillates. This covers diesel and heating oil, the fuels behind trucking, farming, industry and home heating. Distillates are especially closely watched at the moment because diesel prices are at record highs. A draw would suggest the shortage is not yet easing, while an unexpected build could offer some relief. Refinery utilisation and refinery runs. Refinery runs are the amount of crude refineries actually process each day. Utilisation expresses those runs as a share of total operating capacity. At around 92%, US refiners are running hard. A dip often reflects seasonal maintenance, which typically picks up in autumn. Utilisation links the crude and product numbers: when refiners run less, they buy less crude, which tends to push crude stocks up and product stocks down. That is the pattern analysts expect this week. Builds, draws and surprises. Markets react less to the absolute size of a build or draw than to the gap against forecasts. A draw when a build was expected, as in the API data, is typically supportive for prices. A smaller-than-expected build can be too. What to watch The key question for Wednesday is whether the EIA confirms the API's crude draw or the analysts' expected build. For product markets, the distillate number matters most: with diesel at record levels and emergency stock releases being organised, any sign that inventories are rebuilding would be closely scrutinised. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Ted Cruz could suffer bruising 'black eye' heading into 2028 with big bet on GOP race
articles.description: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) has thrown himself behind Attorney General Ken Paxton's struggling Senate campaign – a big bet that could backfire on his own presidential ambitions. Politico reported that Cruz has become a "part-time adviser, part-time bundler" for Paxton, who trails Democrat James Talarico in most polls in the race to replace retiring Sen. John Cornyn, and the 55-year-old Cruz's help could cement him as Texas' GOP kingmaker and boost his national profile ahead of a potential 2028 White House run. "But if Paxton fails, it could be a black eye for Cruz," Politico reported. Cruz stayed neutral during Paxton's bruising primary against Cornyn but jumped in after Paxton won the runoff in May. Within a week, Cruz emceed a Washington fundraiser for the nominee, then joined him on a one-day donor swing through Dallas, Houston and Midland that Cruz said brought in $3 million. "It is absolutely critical that Texas stay red, that Republicans keep a majority in the U.S. Senate and the House, and that we elect Ken Paxton instead of James Talarico," Cruz told the publication. "And so I am all in." He has since pitched himself as a bridge between Cornyn's establishment donors and Paxton's MAGA base , telling Politico he's had "hundreds of conversations" with donors. "The case I've been making to donors who previously supported John Cornyn is, at this point, it's a binary choice, and I think the choice is very clear," Cruz said. Cruz's super PAC, Truth and Courage, reserved more than $2 million in anti-Talarico ads, though that spending has been dwarfed by bigger buys from the Senate Leadership Fund and other GOP groups. Cruz has also hosted fundraisers for Paxton, including one in a Dallas high-rise so packed that Paxton staffers were relegated to the balcony. But Democrats are increasingly optimistic that this is the year they finally flip a Texas Senate seat, and a Paxton loss could give Cruz's would-be 2028 rivals an opening to lay the blame at his feet, Politico reported. One longtime Texas Republican strategist not affiliated with either man argued Cruz has insulated himself. "This is smart on Ted's part," the strategist said. "It cements him with Paxton supporters as being the guy who stood up for him, and it allows him to expand his reach and have a greater claim on having a unified Texas behind him if he makes a run in 2028." If Paxton loses, the strategist added, "he put his best foot forward, and it's going to be Paxton's fault that he lost, not Ted Cruz's." Paxton's campaign declined to comment.
